title: Chemical equilibrium
note: At equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal, and the reaction quotient Q equals the constant K. Write K as products over reactants, each raised to its coefficient, leaving out pure solids and liquids. If Q < K the reaction moves forward; if Q > K it moves back. Le Chatelier: a stressed equilibrium shifts to partly undo the stress, and only temperature changes K.

read.title: A balance that keeps moving
text: Many reactions do not run to completion. As products build up, the reverse reaction speeds up, until the forward and reverse reactions run at the same rate. From then on the concentrations stay constant even though molecules keep reacting in both directions. This is dynamic equilibrium.

The equilibrium constant K captures where that balance lies. For a general reaction, K is the product concentrations over the reactant concentrations, each raised to its coefficient. Pure solids and liquids are left out because their concentrations do not change. A large K means mostly products at equilibrium; a small K means mostly reactants. K says nothing about speed.

At any moment you can compute the same ratio from the actual concentrations; this is the reaction quotient Q. If Q is less than K, there are too few products and the reaction moves forward. If Q is greater than K, it moves backward.

Le Chatelier's principle predicts responses to change. Add a reactant and the system uses some of it up by making more product. Squeeze a gas mixture and it shifts toward the side with fewer gas molecules. Heat an exothermic reaction and it shifts back toward reactants, as if heat were a product. Only that last kind of change, temperature, actually changes K. A catalyst changes nothing about the final balance; it only gets there sooner.
